---
title: "Claude Code Skills — A Student Handout"
---

A companion to the in-class slides (`slides/claude-skills-and-mcp.qmd`). The
slides showed you what skills *are* and walked through a few examples that
ship inside Claude. This handout is the next step: a curated catalogue of
real skills you can install and read, a brainstorming framework for
inventing your own, a workflow for testing and refining them, and a section
on *meta-skills* — skills that watch how you work and propose new skills
back to you.

It is meant to be lived with, not read once. Bookmark it, return to it,
suggest additions.

---

## §1 — Why this exists

In class we hit two snags. First, the example skills in the slides
(`pdf`, `docx`, `pptx`, `xlsx`, `skill-creator`, `init`) ship as built-ins
inside Claude Code, so installing them as a learning exercise is a no-op —
you can't see them appear because they were already there. Second,
several of you said you couldn't picture *what skills you'd even want to
build*, which is fair: skill ideas come from friction, and friction comes
from experience. You've only had a few hours of experience.

This document tries to short-circuit both:

- **Concrete starting points** (§2–§3) — places to land and a table of
  ~30 real, externally-built, non-trivial skills with use-case
  framings sourced from the underlying repos.
- **Imagination unlock** (§4) — four lenses for spotting where your own
  workflow is asking to be skill-ified, with worked examples from skills
  we use daily in another context.
- **Iteration discipline** (§5) — a workflow for after-use debriefs so
  that skills get sharper with every invocation rather than rotting.
- **Meta-skills** (§6) — skills whose job is to make your other skills
  better.
- **Cheatsheet** (§7) — the structural minimum of a SKILL.md.

How to read it: §3 is the catalogue, useful as a browsing surface. §4 is
the part to work *through* with your own life in mind. §5 and §6 are the
parts that turn skill-writing from a one-shot novelty into a practice.

---

## §2 — Where to start: three landing pages

Three URLs to open first. Everything else is downstream of these.

**1. [`anthropics/skills`](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) — the
official canon.** Beyond the doc-format skills you saw in the slides,
this repo contains a dozen-plus skills worth reading purely to see what
*good* SKILL.md files look like. Pay particular attention to
`slack-gif-creator` (Simon Willison's favourite teaching example —
notice how it teaches Claude *primitives* like easing and layering
rather than handing it templates), `mcp-builder` (scaffolds new MCP
servers — itself a skill that builds tools), `algorithmic-art` (seeded
p5.js generative art), and `frontend-design` (opinionated UI generation
that picks aesthetic directions instead of defaulting to generic
Tailwind). Install via `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills`.

**2. [`VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills`](https://github.com/VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills)
— the largest hand-curated index.** The "awesome list" pattern (a
GitHub convention: a curated, opinionated list of links) applied to
skills. VoltAgent's list filters AI-slop entries, organises by domain,
and is cross-agent (skills written for Claude often map cleanly to
Cursor or Gemini). Honourable mentions:
[ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills)
(taxonomy-driven), [travisvn/awesome-claude-skills](https://github.com/travisvn/awesome-claude-skills)
(progressive-disclosure structure), and the tag-faceted browser at
[awesome-skills.com](https://awesome-skills.com/).

**3. [`K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills`](https://github.com/K-Dense-AI/scientific-agent-skills)
— most relevant for this course.** ~135 SKILL.md files across 16
scientific domains: bioinformatics (Scanpy, scVelo, RDKit), neuro,
astronomy (Astropy, FITS), GIS, materials science, plus 78+ scientific
database connectors. For most of you doing scientific computing, this
is the single most directly applicable repo on the internet right now.

For "why skills exist at all" reading, try
[Simon Willison's *Claude Skills are awesome*](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Oct/16/claude-skills/),
[Jesse Vincent's *Skills for Claude!*](https://blog.fsck.com/2025/10/16/skills-for-claude/),
and [Nick Nisi's *Why Everyone Should Try Claude Skills*](https://nicknisi.com/posts/claude-skills/).
For the contrarian view, the
[Hacker News thread #45607117](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45607117)
includes skeptics arguing skills are "a design pattern, not a hard spec."
Read all four — being able to articulate the strongest objection is part
of understanding what you're working with.

## §4 — Brainstorming: spotting your own skill ideas

This is the section to work *through*, not just read. The catalogue tells
you what others built; this tells you how to find what *you* should
build. Four lenses, each with a worked example from skills we use daily
in a different project.

A note on the worked examples: they come from a separate codebase (the
VADE project) where I've spent the last year building out a skill
library for a long-running agent. The skills are project-specific —
don't worry about the names — but the *patterns* transfer. They're here
because they're worked solutions to friction points, and seeing real
solutions makes the lenses easier to apply to your own life.

### Lens 1 — The Boring Repeat Tax

What do you do every week that's about 80% structure and 20% judgment?
The structure part is the skill; the judgment part is what Claude needs
your input on. If you can describe the structure in two paragraphs, you
have a SKILL.md draft.

**Worked example:** the VADE project ships a `day-overview` skill. Every
day a long-running agent does some mix of memo-writing, PR-opening,
file-editing, conversations. At the end of the day, *what shipped?* is a
question you don't want to reconstruct from scratch. The skill walks
through GitHub commits, merged PRs, and decision memos from the day,
classifies them into "wrote", "shipped", "decided", "blocked", and
returns a structured briefing. The judgment part is what Claude
prioritises in the summary; the structure part is the data sources, the
classification scheme, and the output template — all encoded once in
the skill.

For you as a student: what's the weekly structure you keep doing by
hand? A reading-list update? A homework summary? A lab-notebook entry?
A chore log?

### Lens 2 — The Expertise Embedding

What do you have such strong opinions about that a generic prompt would
produce something *wrong*? Wherever you have idiosyncratic standards,
Claude needs to be told them. The skill body is where that knowledge
lives.

**Worked example:** the VADE project ships a `request-briefing` skill
that generates context-handoff documents between work sessions. The
*idiosyncratic* part is the format — what sections, what level of
detail, what verification ritual at the end, which related artifacts to
link. None of those choices are obvious; they're the result of fifty
sessions where the next session got confused because the wrong context
was carried forward. The skill is the cumulative residue of those
mistakes, packaged as a template + an enforcement layer.

For you: what are the conventions in your discipline that "everyone
just knows" but Claude doesn't? APA-style results reporting? A specific
plotting palette? The way your advisor wants commit messages? The
preregistration fields your lab requires? Each of those is a skill.

### Lens 3 — The Documentation Hole

When working with a new framework or library, do you keep re-asking
"where is X documented?" or finding that Claude hallucinates API
signatures? The fix is a docs skill: a SKILL.md that teaches Claude
where to fetch the *real* docs efficiently, and what the common
landmines are.

**Worked example:** the VADE project ships a `quarto-docs` skill. Quarto
is a publishing system whose docs live at `quarto.org`. The naive thing
is to just let Claude search the web; the problem is that Quarto
publishes LLM-optimised markdown bundles at `quarto.org/llms.txt` and
per-page `.llms.md` URLs, and *if you don't tell Claude that*, it'll
fetch HTML, hallucinate YAML keys, or nest options under the wrong
parent (`format.html.sidebar` is wrong; `sidebar` is top-level under
`website`). The skill is one paragraph saying "for Quarto questions,
fetch from these URLs in this order; here are three landmines we've
hit." That's it.

**The generalisable move**: if you're working with a framework or
library that doesn't already have a docs skill, you can build one in 30
minutes. Some big ones already have them (`tldraw`, `Cloudflare
Workers`, the Anthropic SDK). For everything else — your favourite R
package, your numerical library, your astronomy toolkit — you might be
the first person to package its docs as a skill. That's a publishable
contribution to the community.

### Lens 4 — The Ritual / Bookend

What do you always want to do at the start or end of something — a
session, a project, a publishing cycle — but keep forgetting parts of?
Bookend rituals are perfect skill material because the structure is
deterministic and the friction is forgetting.

**Worked example:** the VADE project ships an `end-session` skill. At
the end of every working session you want to commit pending changes,
write a session log, save a working-memory note, sync the semantic
index if memos changed, and consider whether anything from the session
should be externalised as a new skill or operations doc. Doing all six
manually means at least one gets dropped most sessions. The skill is a
checklist: each step runs in order, each is reported, the skill writes
a marker file that suppresses other end-of-session prompts. It turns a
fragile ritual into a reliable one.

For you: what's your end-of-coding-session ritual? Commit, push, write
a TODO for tomorrow, close the laptop. What's your start-of-paper
ritual? Pull literature, scaffold sections, set up the bibliography,
pre-register. Whatever it is — if you keep forgetting parts of it,
that's a skill.

### Domain-by-domain prompts

For each of the lanes below, ask yourself the listed questions. Even one
"yes" is a skill candidate.

**Research.** What's your literature-review tax? Citation-chasing
friction? Notebook hygiene before you forget what a cell does?
Reproducibility audit before submitting? Pre-registration drafting?
Statistical-reporting conformance (do all your `t(df) =` and effect
sizes show up?)?

**Writing.** Voice consistency across a long document? Citation
formatting per journal? Reformatting a Beamer deck as Quarto? Drafting
a referee response? Generating an alt-text pass for accessibility?

**Personal.** Email triage with reply drafting in your voice (drafts
only, never auto-sent)? Meal planning from what's in your fridge? Trip
prep with weather-aware packing? Gift-list management? Birthday
reminders with context on what each person likes?

**Hobby.** Rule-grounded play (D&D, board games, chess analysis)?
Spaced-repetition for any skill you're learning? Coaching for fitness or
music practice? Plant-care logging? A cooking-from-the-pantry brain?

**Teaching.** Rubric-grading with explicit criteria? Quiz generation
from lecture notes? Exam scaffolding with point distributions? Office-
hours triage that points students at the right resource?

### Three meta-prompts

If none of the lenses are biting, try these three abstract questions:

1. **"What would I delegate to a smart intern who doesn't know my
   context?"** The SKILL.md is the briefing you'd write that intern.
2. **"What context do I reload into Claude every time I start a session
   about X?"** That repeated context is the skill body.
3. **"What did I fix in Claude's output the last three times in the
   same way?"** Whatever you keep correcting is the enforcement layer
   the skill needs.

## §5 — Iterating on a skill: the author–test–refine loop

Authoring a skill is the first ten percent. The other ninety is testing
it, watching it fail, and refining it. Treat it as a four-step loop you
run after every meaningful invocation.

### A. First-use observation

Did Claude actually invoke the skill when you expected it to? Did you
have to nudge ("use the skills/foo skill")? If you nudged, the
**description is wrong** — either too narrow (didn't match the situation)
or too vague (model didn't recognise the trigger). Description quality
is the single biggest determinant of whether a skill fires reliably.

Did the skill body actually help, or did Claude essentially do its
default behaviour anyway? If the latter, ask whether the skill has a
job at all — if Claude's defaults already cover it, the skill is
redundant.

### B. After-use debrief — ask the model directly

After the task is done, run this prompt against Claude with the
session still loaded. It works best because the model can introspect
on what just happened.

::: {.callout-tip title="Skill debrief prompt"}
We just used the `<skill-name>` skill on `<task>`. Walk me through:

1. Which parts of the SKILL.md were actually load-bearing for solving
   the task?
2. What was in the SKILL.md that I ignored or didn't need?
3. What did I wish was in there but wasn't — what would have made the
   task easier?
4. Did the description accurately match the task, or was the trigger
   loose / tight?
5. If you were rewriting this skill from scratch based on this one
   use, what would you change?

Be specific — quote phrases from the SKILL.md you're talking about.
:::

The model will give you concrete, line-level suggestions about its own
behaviour. Take them with a grain of salt (it's introspecting, not
remembering perfectly), but treat the suggestions as a strong prior.
Edit the SKILL.md immediately while the use case is fresh.

### C. The drift check

Skills age. Anthropic ships model updates monthly; what was load-bearing
a month ago might be table stakes the model now does by default.
Reverse: a skill that worked great might stop firing because the
description vocabulary no longer matches how the model categorises
tasks.

Every few weeks, take an old skill you haven't touched. Try to invoke it
on a task you know it should match. Did it fire? Did it work? If not,
prune the description, prune the body, or retire the skill.

### D. Split, retire, or fold

When a skill grows past one job, **split** it. A SKILL.md that does
"PDF analysis *and* OCR *and* citation extraction" should be three
skills, each with a tight description.

When two skills overlap so much that you forget which one to invoke,
**fold** one into the other.

When a skill stops firing for three weeks running, ask whether the
trigger is wrong (rewrite the description) or the need has gone away
(**retire** it). Dead skills clutter the model's selection space.

### Common pitfalls

A short list of failure modes worth recognising:

- **Description too generic.** Fires on everything; pollutes the skill
  selection. Fix: name the *trigger condition* concretely. "Use when
  editing Quarto frontmatter" beats "Use for documentation work."
- **Description too specific.** Never fires because the model doesn't
  categorise tasks the way you do. Fix: include synonyms and example
  triggers.
- **Body duplicates Claude's defaults.** Adds nothing the model wouldn't
  do anyway. Fix: focus the body on what's *non-obvious* — the
  landmines, the conventions, the references you'd otherwise have to
  re-explain.
- **Wraps a script that isn't tested.** The skill calls
  `scripts/foo.sh` but no one runs the script directly. When it breaks,
  the skill silently fails. Fix: keep the script runnable on its own
  and test it independently.
- **Hidden environment dependency.** "Just install
  `imagemagick` and `ffmpeg` and `pandoc` and …" If it's not in the
  default environment, document it loudly at the top of the SKILL.md.

## §6 — Meta-skills: skills that improve other skills

This is the part most people miss. Once you have a few skills, the next
move isn't to write more skills — it's to write skills *about* your
skills. Meta-skills make the skill-writing practice scale.

### What a meta-skill does

A meta-skill takes the place of you-the-author. Instead of you running
the §5 debrief loop manually, a meta-skill watches what just happened,
asks the right questions, and suggests improvements (or proposes new
skills). Three concrete patterns:

**1. The skill-debrief skill.** Wraps the §5.B prompt as an invocable
skill. After any non-trivial task, type `/skill-debrief` and the skill
walks Claude through its own retrospective: which skills fired, which
should have but didn't, where you nudged manually, what was missing.
The output is a structured note you can paste into a `skills-ideas.md`
or directly into a SKILL.md edit. Saves you the cognitive load of
remembering to debrief.

**2. The skill-creator skill.** This one ships with Claude Code as
`/skill-creator`. It's a meta-skill in the strongest sense: it walks you
through *authoring* a new skill — interrogating you for the trigger
condition, drafting the description, scaffolding the body, registering
the file in the right directory. Use it. Even when you think you know
the skill you want to write, having Claude interview you about the
edge cases produces a tighter SKILL.md than typing one from scratch.

**3. The friction logger.** A skill (or a hook) that watches your
session for *unrecognised* friction — moments where you re-explained
the same context, where you reached for a CLI Claude doesn't know
about, where you fixed the same kind of output twice. At end of session
it produces a list: "you did X three times, consider packaging it." The
VADE project does a version of this in its `end-session` ritual: one
of the steps is "did anything in this session produce a recurring
pattern, repeated friction, or transferable insight that future
sessions would benefit from having pre-packaged?" If yes, file an issue
or invoke the skill-creator. The emancipatory logic is straightforward:
giving back to the substrate is part of using it well.

### Why meta-skills matter

Without meta-skills, your skill library grows linearly with your
attention budget — you only add skills when you happen to remember to.
With meta-skills, your library grows from *every session you don't
remember*, because the meta-skill is doing the noticing. The meta-skill
is the part of your future that watches your present.

### The simplest meta-skill you can write today

Open a file `~/skills-ideas.md`. Whenever you finish a coding session,
ask Claude:

> "Looking at what we just did, are there any 5-minute improvements I
> could make to my skills? Anything I re-explained, anything you
> fumbled, anything I corrected more than once? Write it as a list of
> proposed skill ideas with one-sentence descriptions, and append to
> `~/skills-ideas.md` if I confirm."

That's not a packaged skill yet — it's a manually-invoked prompt — but
it's the seed. Once you've appended a dozen ideas, package the prompt
itself as `/skills-debrief` and the practice becomes durable.

### Meta-skills as a research direction

This area is genuinely under-explored. Most published skills are
object-level (do task X). Few are reflexive (improve other skills X).
If you wanted a small student project that would be a real
contribution to the community, building a polished `/skill-debrief` or
`/skill-drift-check` and publishing it as a repo would be a good one.
The lens 4 example earlier (`end-session`) is in this category, and so
is the official `/skill-creator` — but the space between them is wide
open.

---

## §7 — Cheatsheet appendix

The structural minimum to write a skill.

### SKILL.md frontmatter

```yaml
---
name: my-skill-slug
description: Use when [trigger condition]. [What the skill does in one
  sentence — make sure the trigger words a model would naturally reach
  for are present.]
---
```

### Where skills live

- **User-level**: `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` — available
  in every project.
- **Project-level**: `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` in the
  repo — checked in, shared with collaborators.
- **Plugins**: `/plugin marketplace add <github-owner>/<repo>` then
  `/plugin install <plugin-name>` — for skills shipped as marketplace
  bundles (this is how `anthropics/skills` works).

### Description-writing micro-rules

1. **Lead with the trigger condition** ("Use when…" / "Trigger
   on…"). The model selects skills by matching the description to the
   current task.
2. **Name synonyms.** If you call it "literature review" and the user
   says "lit review", the skill might miss. Include both.
3. **State what the skill is *not* for** if there's a near-miss skill
   it shouldn't poach from.

### Capture mechanism for skill ideas

A `~/skills-ideas.md` file. One line per idea, written the moment it
occurs. Don't let the perfect SKILL.md be the enemy of the noticed
friction.
